summary:
Egypt presents a direct and documented entry risk to trans visitors. The Ministry of Interior holds broad powers under the immigration law to refuse entry to, or deport, anyone whose presence is said to disturb public order and morality, and those powers have been applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that law and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents between 2018 and 2022. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights separately records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even where no charge is ever upheld. Removal therefore does not require any offence under Egyptian law.

Same-sex conduct is not expressly written into the penal statutes, but prosecutions are a routine outcome rather than a theoretical one. Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961. Court of Cassation interpretations from the 1970s had already removed the requirement of a financial exchange: habitual or multiple partners sufficed to sustain a charge.

Police run entrapment operations against people they identify as queer. A BBC investigation, "How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps", found officers using fake accounts on dating applications, with victims describing blackmail and arrest; the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights documents the same pattern and identifies transgender women as a particular target. Bedayaa records coerced anal examinations carried out during arrests and states that authorities turn a blind eye to the practice.

Legal gender recognition is being actively closed. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide on 12 December 2024 closes the loophole in Civil Status Law 143/1994 that had allowed transgender Egyptians to correct gender markers through governorate committees. A trans visitor should expect no route to a corrected document in Egypt, and should expect documents issued elsewhere to be treated as evidence rather than as settled fact.

There is no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. Outright International's country overview (updated 12 March 2026) confirms that vague public-morality and debauchery provisions are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences despite the absence of an explicit sodomy offence. TIMEP's submission for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle (6 January 2025) records that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health, with barriers to equitable services persisting since the previous cycle and pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

Morality and public order provisions reach expression as well as conduct. The relevant provisions criminalise any behaviour, or the expression of any idea, deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, giving police broad leeway to prosecute LGBTQ expression. In 2017 the Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order preventing the appearance of homosexuals or the promotion of their slogans in media, and legislation introduced in August 2018 placed any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws.

Detention carries documented physical risk. Human Rights Watch, in "In a Time of Torture" (29 February 2004), documented the Queen Boat-era crackdown, including arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings motivated by sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants. Bedayaa records rising arrests of homosexual and trans people alongside coerced examinations, and the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights reports that violations continue inside police stations.

Personal and family law follows the religious law of the person's recognised religion, Islam or Coptic Orthodox Christianity, neither of which recognises same-sex relationships; Egyptian law therefore recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. Where a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has a documented history of mass action. Following the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, television hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against the community, with Moussa publishing personal information of flag-raisers; at least 84 people were arrested between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many subjected to forced anal tests. In December 2014 the presenter Mona Iraqi collaborated with police on a raid on a public bathhouse that arrested around 26 men, all later acquitted. In January 2019 Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his programme.

Earlier episodes show the same machinery. In 2013 a comedian was charged by the Morsi government with propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity. In 2009 the newspaper Al Balagh Al Gadid was shut down and two reporters jailed for printing a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a 17-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labour, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site.

Social climate is a compounding factor rather than a legal one. Pew Research Center found that 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and polling suggests only a minority support LGBTQ rights; as a result Egyptian political parties and human rights NGOs do not express public support. The term 'khawalat', historically referring to male cross-dressing dancers, has been stigmatised and is used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men. State officials and police are recorded as routinely harassing, abusing and torturing LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, leading to unfair arrests and abuse in custody.

The September 2017 crackdown caused a state of trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ individuals, with many attempted suicides. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, fled abroad, was granted asylum and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBTQ youths and individuals have left the country because of social and political threats.

Activism has grown without legal change. After the 2011 revolution LGBTQ activists became more visible and online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia went viral on Twitter and Facebook by 2013, but this did not translate into legal reform.
localsOnly:
The 12 December 2024 Ministry of Interior directive is addressed to civil-registry heads nationwide and binds Egyptian citizens seeking to correct gender markers, closing the route that Civil Status Law 143/1994 had provided through governorate committees. Residents therefore lose the only administrative path to legal gender recognition, with no statutory alternative established in its place.

Residents live without any anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and without a complaints mechanism grounded in those grounds. Bedayaa's reference material for SOGIESC work documents detention conditions and the specific situation of trans people under this framework.

Healthcare is a documented hardship for residents. TIMEP records discriminatory laws, policies and practices affecting the right to health of transgender and intersex Egyptians, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare settings and barriers that have persisted across UPR cycles.

Marriage and personal status are determined by the religious law of the person's recognised religion, so residents in same-sex relationships have no route to recognition, and a relationship that becomes public can be introduced as evidence in a criminal indictment.

Public opinion constrains advocacy: with 95% of Egyptians surveyed saying homosexuality should not be accepted by society, political parties and human rights organisations do not express public support, and the 2011-era visibility of activists and viral online campaigns by 2013 produced no legislative reform.
outOfScopeNotes:
The full text of the 12 December 2024 Ministry of Interior directive is not reproduced in the sources consulted here; its scope, any transitional provisions and any appeal route for Egyptians who had already corrected markers remain unresolved.

No source in this inventory gives a count of entry refusals or deportations of trans travellers in a defined recent period. The 12 incidents analysed by Cairo 52 cover 2018 to 2022, and the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights describes the practice without figures; the current rate is not sourced.

Whether Economic Court rulings reading the Penal Code together with Article 9(C) of Law 10/1961 are applied uniformly across all governorates, and how frequently they are used against foreign visitors rather than residents, is not established by these sources.

The frequency and current authorisation status of coerced anal examinations are documented qualitatively by Bedayaa and Human Rights Watch but are not quantified here, and no sourced statement confirms whether the 2017 media-regulator order remains formally in force.

TIMEP frames its health findings as a submission to Egypt's fourth UPR cycle; the outcome of that cycle and any resulting commitments are not sourced in this inventory.
